doc.title: Allan Vaché interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

title: Father's support and 17 years with the Jim Cullum band
summary: His father backed his choice; he took a steady job at 22 with Cullum for 17 years, left burned out and had lean years.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: And your father was supportive in you guys going in this direction?

Yeah, very much so. I worked with so many friends who tell me how their parents were very much opposed to them going into becoming professional musicians because this business is a crap shoot. Whether or not you’re going to be able to make a living at it is very questionable, and a lot of guys can’t make a living at it. I have to say that I consider myself fairly lucky. When I was 22 I took a steady job, stayed there for 17 years, and worked with a band working in a night club six nights a week and traveling, the Jim Cullum Jazz Band in San Antonio. So I was with them for 17 years. And I mean I got pretty burned out on it after so many years and I left. And I figured I was taking a pretty good chance, because here I was, I was off the circuit for a long time and then trying to break into the circuit. I had a couple of fairly lean years. But I was lucky enough that — I like to think that maybe my ability had something to do with it — but I was able to eventually break into the circuit and do pretty well. I’m not getting rich, but so far I don’t have any bill collectors pounding on my doors so I can’t complain too much. If you can do that I think you do okay in this business.

Someone was asking me the other day what’s the definition of making it big? Sometimes kids use that phrase. And I think you almost just defined it. If you’re doing what you love, that’s a big step right there.
Well it’s like the joke what do you call a jazz musician without a girlfriend? Homeless. It’s funny but unfortunately in many cases it’s true.
